metric_rationale: To cleanly discriminate between Take The Best (TTB) and Tallying, we should focus exclusively on the trials where their predictions diverge. This metric dynamically computes the TTB and Tallying predictions for each trial, filters for trials where the two heuristics predict different choices, and calculates the proportion of subject responses that align with TTB. Under TTB, this metric will be close to 1.0 (subject to noise), while under Tallying, it will be close to 0.0.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic on trials where Tallying and Take The Best (TTB) make strictly opposing deterministic predictions. The experimental design specifically includes trials where an option is favored by the single highest-validity discriminating cue (TTB's choice) but the other option is favored by a sheer majority of lower-validity cues (Tallying's choice). By isolating these conflicting trials, we expect data generated by Tallying to score close to 1.0, whereas data generated by TTB will score close to 0.0, yielding maximum discriminability.

To maximally discriminate Take The Best (TTB) from Weighted Additive (WADD) models, we isolate 'conflict trials' where the single best discriminating cue points to one option, but the sum of all lower-validity cues points to the other. TTB will consistently choose the option favored by the best cue (yielding a metric near 1.0), whereas WADD (particularly at lower values of gamma) will compensate and choose the other option, drastically lowering its match rate with TTB's predictions. By focusing exclusively on these conflict trials, we amplify the divergence between the two theories and suppress noise from trials where both models agree.

The metric computes the covariance between the relative number of supporting cues (sum of A's features minus sum of B's features) and the probability of choosing Option A. For Take The Best (TTB), the choice is determined entirely by the first cue, which always favors A in this design. Thus, TTB predicts a flat probability of choosing A across all trials, yielding a covariance near zero. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all cues, so the probability of choosing A increases monotonically as the net number of supporting cues shifts in A's favor, yielding a strongly positive covariance.

This metric calculates the difference in the rate of Take-The-Best (TTB) consistent choices between trials where the first discriminating cue is at depth 0 versus depth 3. Theory 1 predicts a sharp, explicit decay in TTB usage as depth increases (due to its gamma parameter), leading to a large positive difference. Theory 2 (WADD) evaluates options continuously without a discrete switch, so its choice probabilities will behave differently across the depth gradient.

This metric exploits a structural symmetry in the Competing Theory (Context-Dependent Strategy Selection) that WADD strictly breaks. In both Trial 1 and Trial 4, the first discriminating cue is at depth 0, meaning the probability of using TTB is identical. Furthermore, in both trials, Option A has exactly 1 fewer positive feature than Option B, meaning the Tallying strategy's softmax probability for Option A is also mathematically identical (since it depends only on the difference in sums, which is -1 in both cases). Thus, the Competing Theory predicts exactly the same probability of choosing A for both trials, yielding an expected difference of 0. In contrast, WADD integrates the non-linear weights of all features. The difference in weighted evidence for Trial 1 vs Trial 4 is rigorously non-zero (specifically, 2*(0.7^g) - 0.6^g - 0.5^g > 0), so WADD reliably predicts a higher probability of choosing A in Trial 1 than in Trial 4.

By taking advantage of the experimental design, we compute the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between trials where the TTB direction and Tallying scores are identical but the specific lower-validity cues change. Under the Constant-Mixture (TTB + Tallying) theory, the choice probability depends only on the TTB direction and the Tallying score difference, both of which are constant across these trial pairs; hence, the expected difference is 0. Under the WADD theory, choice probability is sensitive to the exact validities of the cues, so shifting the support to lower-validity cues strictly decreases the option's overall value. Summing the expected positive contrasts across three different trial groupings yields a metric that is near 0 for TTB+Tallying and robustly positive for WADD.

This metric calculates the difference in choice probability for the TTB-favored option (the one with the single highest validity cue) when it is pitted against a 'weak' Tallying competitor (cues 3 and 4) versus a 'strong' Tallying competitor (cues 2 and 3). Theory 2 (Constant-Mixture) predicts a difference of exactly zero, because in both cases TTB favors the single-cue option and Tallying favors the two-cue option by exactly the same margin of wins (1 vs 2). Theory 1 (WADD) computes a continuous weighted sum using objective validities, meaning the 'strong' competitor will genuinely reduce the choice probability of the single-cue option compared to the 'weak' competitor, predicting a positive difference.
